global.headline: IRAN OFFERS $30,000 BOUNTY TO KILL OR CAPTURE US SOLDIERS AS TRUMP SCALES BACK SOUTH KOREA DRILLS AND QATAR PILOT ROW DEEPENS
summary: Iran's army chief, Major General Amir Hatami, announced Sunday a bounty of US$30,000 for killing or capturing a US soldier — doubled to US$60,000 if carried out by a woman — telling state news agency IRNA the reward scheme followed "a large number of requests" from people wanting to contribute financially to the war effort. The announcement, made at a ceremony honouring journalists, comes with no US ground forces deployed inside Iran beyond a single April mission to rescue a downed American pilot; the war, which began 28 February with a joint US-Israel strike that killed Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei, has been fought almost entirely from the air and sea since a roughly 40-day April ceasefire collapsed and June's peace framework fell apart.

Iran's dispute with mediator Qatar over three captured Su-24 pilots sharpened further: Iranian General Mohammad Bagherzadeh's letter to the Red Cross said Javad Salehi, Abdolmajid Dashtian and Omran Behraveshian had been held incommunicado for six months without family or diplomatic access since their bombers were shot down over Qatar in March. Qatari foreign ministry spokesman Majed Al Ansari again "categorically" denied holding any surviving pilots, saying search-and-rescue teams found and offered to return only one pilot's remains, and that Doha's invitation for Iran to review its search operation's details has gone unanswered.

Trump ordered Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to substantially scale back this week's planned 11-day US-South Korea joint military exercises — involving 18,000 South Korean troops — after Seoul declined his request to help pressure Iran into denuclearising. "They said, 'No thanks!'" Trump wrote, calling the drills "costly" and a "hostile" signal toward North Korea's Kim Jong Un, with whom he cited a good relationship. Separately, the aircraft carrier USS Abraham Lincoln headed home after 265 days deployed supporting the war, with CENTCOM commander Admiral Brad Cooper acknowledging reported mental-health strain among the crew even as he said the carrier has among the lowest case numbers of the US Navy's 11 active carriers.
global.geopolitical: A cash bounty on American troops, a South Korea drill scaled back explicitly over Seoul's refusal to help pressure Iran, and a fraying relationship with mediator Qatar together show a war nearly six months old radiating consequences into US alliance management on the opposite side of the world, not just the Gulf.
global.socioeconomic: The bounty offer and the prolonged carrier deployment both point to a war effort straining under its own duration — Iran resorting to crowdsourced cash incentives even as it fights largely without a functioning air force, and the US Navy publicly defending crew welfare after 265 days at sea supporting a campaign with no clear end in sight.

global.headline: KUSHNER MEETS HAMAS LEADER IN EGYPT TO SALVAGE GAZA ROAD MAP BEFORE NETANYAHU TALKS
summary: Jared Kushner, Trump's son-in-law and Middle East envoy, held a rare direct meeting with Hamas political leader Khalil al-Hayya in Egypt on Sunday, joined by Egyptian intelligence chief Hassan Rashad, Qatari diplomat Ali Al Thawadi and a senior Turkish official, in a bid to secure Hamas's commitment to the 15-point Gaza road map — particularly its disarmament terms — before Kushner meets Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Monday.

A Palestinian source told Al Jazeera that Hamas's leadership used the meeting to brief Kushner on what it called Israeli ceasefire violations; a Hamas official said the group remains committed to the plan and is waiting for mediators to open the 14-day negotiation period meant to produce an implementation timetable. Netanyahu, who formally rejected the Hamas-signed plan on 9 August, is under pressure from Washington to re-engage even as Israeli officials continue to call the document short of "complete demilitarisation."
global.geopolitical: A face-to-face Kushner-Hamas meeting — unusual for a US administration that treats Hamas as a terrorist organisation — signals Washington judges direct pressure on the group's own leadership, not just Israel, necessary to revive a plan that has sat rejected for a week; Monday's Netanyahu meeting will show whether that pressure extends to Israel too.
global.socioeconomic: Any credible movement toward Hamas's actual disarmament and an Israeli withdrawal timeline would be the first concrete step toward Gaza's reconstruction and governance transition since Hamas signed the plan two weeks ago, implementation of which has otherwise stalled entirely.

global.headline: UKRAINE LAUNCHES ONE OF ITS LARGEST DRONE ATTACKS OF THE WAR ON MOSCOW REGION, KILLING AT LEAST SIX
summary: Ukraine launched one of its largest aerial attacks of the war overnight into Sunday, sending more than 800 drones toward Russia; Moscow region governor Andrei Vorobyov said an 83-year-old man was killed and several people injured when a warehouse belonging to online retailer Wildberries was struck in Podolsk, with further damage reported at a warehouse near Domodedovo airport, one of Moscow's main gateways. Russian state news agency TASS called it the largest Ukrainian drone attack since the start of the year, with the barrage concentrated on the Moscow region where much of Russia's elite lives.

Russia's defence ministry said it shot down more than 800 drones nationwide overnight, with at least six people confirmed killed across the country. It was at least the seventh reported strike on Wildberries logistics infrastructure since mid-July, part of Ukraine's sustained campaign against Russian retail and warehouse targets.
global.geopolitical: Striking so close to Moscow itself, rather than border regions or occupied territory, keeps pressure on the Kremlin's ability to shield the capital and its own elite from the war's costs, even as ceasefire talks remain stalled.
global.socioeconomic: Repeated strikes on Wildberries — Russia's largest online retailer — chip directly at civilian retail and logistics capacity inside Russia, a deliberate economic-pressure campaign distinct from purely military targeting.

global.headline: ZAMBIA VOTE COUNT REACHES QUARTER MARK AS OBSERVERS DOCUMENT WIDESPREAD INTIMIDATION AND VIOLENCE
summary: Zambia's Electoral Commission released partial results covering 49 of 226 constituencies late Saturday, showing President Hakainde Hichilema leading with 438,708 votes (52.6 per cent) to challenger Brian Mundubile's 351,281 (42.1 per cent), as counting continued under heightened security following Friday's violence-triggered suspension.

The SADC observer mission said it had recorded reports of intimidation, assault, abduction and property damage across five provinces, with one submission alleging fatalities — the fullest independent account yet of the violence that halted counting. Mundubile, without providing evidence, again claimed victory and alleged military personnel had taken control of tallying centres in Mufulira, that result forms had gone missing, and that officials in North-Western Province were told to stop releasing results; Hichilema stopped short of declaring victory but described his campaign's results as "encouraging."
global.geopolitical: An international observer mission formally documenting violence and alleged fatalities — rather than merely noting the commission's own suspension — raises the diplomatic stakes on however the count concludes, and on whether Hichilema's likely re-election is seen as legitimate by SADC and the EU.
global.socioeconomic: As Africa's second-largest copper producer, continued uncertainty over the count's integrity risks unsettling the mining investment central to Hichilema's debt-restructuring programme, even as the numbers so far point toward the market-friendly outcome investors have been expecting.

global.headline: INDONESIA EARTHQUAKE DEATH TOLL RISES TO 51 AS RESCUERS REACH ISOLATED FLORES VILLAGES
summary: The death toll from Saturday's magnitude-7.7 earthquake off Flores island rose to 51 by Sunday, Indonesian authorities said, as rescue teams cleared landslide-blocked roads to reach previously isolated villages in East Nusa Tenggara province. Thirty-six people were seriously injured and 77 more suffered minor injuries; at least 346 houses were damaged, including 157 severely, and more than 230 aftershocks have been recorded, the strongest measuring magnitude 6.2.

Singapore Prime Minister Lawrence Wong conveyed condolences to Indonesia over the earthquake, one of several public messages of sympathy from regional leaders as the disaster's toll continued to climb through the weekend.
global.geopolitical: A slowly climbing toll and reopening roads mark the shift from acute rescue to a longer recovery phase testing Jakarta's reach into one of its more remote, disaster-exposed eastern provinces.
global.socioeconomic: With hundreds of homes damaged and villages still cut off, the reconstruction burden falls on communities already among Indonesia's least economically connected, extending the disaster's cost well beyond its immediate death toll.

singapore.headline: MALAYSIA ISSUES ARREST WARRANT FOR SINGAPORE BUSINESSMAN IN MACC PROBE; HE DENIES 'RUNNING AWAY'
summary: A Kuala Lumpur magistrate's court issued an arrest warrant on 4 August for Singapore-based businessman Poh Po Lian, co-founder of Malaysian hotel group WazLian Group, after Malaysia's Anti-Corruption Commission (MACC) said he had remained untraceable for three years despite promising ten months ago to meet investigators. Malaysian national Jennifer Kok Sau Keng was issued a warrant in the same case; MACC said it had previously tried to locate both, including at a Singapore address, without success.

Poh rejected the characterisation on Sunday, saying "I have never 'run away' and any accusation in this regard is false," and that he had continued cooperating with Malaysian authorities — visiting MACC's Johor Bahru office in March to give a statement, attending a Kuala Lumpur probate hearing the same month as executor of a deceased Malaysian tycoon's estate, and having his solicitors formally request a case review in late March.
singapore.geopolitical: A Singapore-based businessman facing a foreign arrest warrant over an unspecified corruption probe underlines the cross-border legal exposure Singapore residents doing business in Malaysia can carry, even while contesting the process from Singapore soil.
singapore.socioeconomic: The dispute over whether Poh evaded or cooperated with investigators — a gap the public record cannot yet resolve — leaves the underlying corruption allegations against his hotel business unresolved, a reputational overhang for WazLian Group regardless of how the warrant is eventually executed.

singapore.headline: NEW SCHEME SENDS TRAINED VOLUNTEERS TO CHECK ON JURONG PATIENTS WITH SERIOUS ORGAN FAILURE
summary: A new scheme launched in Jurong will send trained volunteers from Loving Heart Multi-Service Centre to check on patients with serious organ failure in their own homes, extending community-based support to a group of patients whose conditions typically require frequent monitoring.
singapore.socioeconomic: Community-volunteer models like this aim to catch complications early and ease the burden on Singapore's hospital system from a chronically ill patient group that would otherwise rely on repeat emergency visits, part of a broader push to shift routine monitoring out of acute-care settings.

word.definition: The quality of being open to bribery or corruption; readiness to sacrifice principle for money.
word.etymology: From Latin venalis, "for sale," from venum ("a thing for sale") + -alis; entered English in the mid-17th century via French vénal.
word.example: Iran's army chief converting soldiers' deaths into a cash transaction — US$30,000 a kill, doubled if the killer is a woman — turns battlefield violence into a matter of pure venality.
